In the Hadith of the Slander, it is related that this verse, up to ten verses, were revealed concerning the story of ʿĀʾisha. We have mentioned the Hadith of the Slander in the book "al-Hadaʾiq" and in the book "al-Mughni fi al-Tafsir," but we did not lengthen its mention here, because our purpose is to abridge this book so that it may be memorized. As for al-ifk, it is falsehood, and al-ʿusba is the group.

The meaning of His saying ﴿among you﴾ is: among the believers. ʿUrwa related from ʿĀʾisha that she said: "They were four: Hassan ibn Thabit, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy [ibn Salul], Mistah ibn Uthatha, and Hamna bint Jahsh." Muqatil also counted them thus.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not consider it bad for you﴾. The exegetes said: this is an address to ʿĀʾisha and Safwan ibn al-Muʿattal. It was said: it is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and ʿĀʾisha. The meaning is: you will be rewarded for it. ﴿For every person among them﴾, meaning: of the lying band, ﴿is what he has earned of sin﴾, i.e., the recompense for the wrong he committed according to the extent of his immersion in it. ﴿And he who took upon himself its greater part among them﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Razin, ʿIkrima, Mujahid, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, al-Hasan, and Mahbub from Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read "kibrahu" with a damma on the kaf. al-Kisaʾi said: both are dialects (lughatan). Ibn Qutayba said: kibr al-shayʾ is its greater part, and this verse is an example of it. Qays ibn al-Khatim said, describing a woman:

She sleeps through the greater part of her affairs, then when she rises slowly, she nearly is unrecognizable.

Regarding the one who took upon himself that role, there are two opinions.

One: he is ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿUrwa from ʿĀʾisha, and this was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Muqatil. The exegetes said: he is the one who spread the story, so for him is a great punishment in the Fire. al-Dahhak said: he is the one who began it.

It was said to her: "O Mother of the Believers, does not Allah say: ﴿And he who took upon himself its greater part among them, for him is a great punishment﴾?" She said: "Has his sight not gone?" Masruq related from her that she said: "What punishment is greater than blindness? Perhaps Allah will make that great punishment the loss of his sight," meaning Hassan ibn Thabit.

Then, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, rebuked those who engaged in the slander by His saying: ﴿Why, when you heard it, did the believers (al-mu'minun) and the believing women (al-mu'minat) not think good of themselves﴾, i.e., why did you not, when you heard the slander against ʿĀʾisha, O lying band — ﴿the believers﴾ from the lying band, namely Hassan and Mistah — ﴿and the believing women﴾, namely Hamna bint Jahsh — ﴿of themselves﴾. There are three opinions regarding this: One: of their mothers. Two: of their sisters. Three: of the people of their religion, because the believers are like a single soul. ﴿And said, "This is a clear falsehood"﴾, i.e., a manifest lie. It is mentioned in the tafsir that Abu Ayyub al-Ansari's wife said to him: "Have you not heard what people are saying about the matter of ʿĀʾisha?" He said: "This is a clear falsehood. Would you, O mother, have done such a thing?" She said: "God forbid!" He said: "By Allah, ʿĀʾisha is better than you," and then this verse was revealed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿None of you would ever have been pure﴾ — al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Qatāda read "mā zakkā" with the kāf shaddah (doubled).

Regarding those addressed by this, there are two opinions:

One of them: it is general, addressing all creation. The second: it is specific to those who spoke in the slander (al-ifk).

Then, regarding its meaning, there are four opinions:

The first: "he would not have been guided (mā ihtadā)," narrated by Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbās. The second: "he would not have embraced Islam (mā aslama)," said by Ibn Zayd. The third: "he would not have become righteous (mā ṣalaḥa)," said by Muqātil. The fourth: "he would not have been purified (mā ṭahhara)," said by Ibn Qutayba.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But Allah purifies whom He wills﴾ — that is, He purifies whom He wills from sin through repentance and forgiveness. So the meaning is: "And I have willed to accept your repentance." ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾ — He knows what is in your souls of repentance and regret.

The exegetes said: the occasion of its revelation was that Abu Bakr al-Siddiq used to spend on Mistah, because of his kinship and poverty. When he got involved in the matter of 'A'ishah, Abu Bakr said: "By God, I will never spend on him anything ever again." So this verse was revealed. As for al-fadl, Abu 'Ubaydah said it means bounty (al-tafaddul), and al-sa'ah means abundance (al-jiddah). The exegetes said: what is meant by it is Abu Bakr.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that they should give⦆. Ibn Qutaybah said: its meaning is "that they should not give," so the "la" (لا) has been omitted. The exegetes said: when Abu Bakr heard ﴿Do you not love that God should forgive you?⦆ he said, "Yes, my Lord," and he restored his spending on Mistah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 24, verse 30–31:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Tell the believing men to lower their gaze﴾, concerning "min" (from) there are two opinions.

One of them: it is redundant (ṣilah). The second: it is essential (aṣl), because they were not commanded to lower their gaze absolutely, but were commanded to lower it from what is not lawful.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and guard their private parts﴾, there are two opinions. One: from what is not lawful for them; this was said by the majority (al-jumhur). The second: from being seen, so it is a command to them to conceal themselves; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾ refers to lowering the gaze and guarding the private parts. ﴿It is purer for them﴾, that is, better and more excellent. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what they do﴾, regarding the gaze and the private parts. Then He commanded the women with what He commanded the men.

(p-31) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And not to display their adornment﴾, that is, not to show it to non-mahram men. Their adornment is of two kinds: hidden, such as bracelets, earrings, armlets, necklaces and the like; and apparent, which is what is indicated by His saying: ﴿except what appears thereof﴾. Concerning this there are seven opinions.

One of them: it is the clothing; this was narrated by Abu al-Ahwas from Ibn Mas'ud; and in another wording he said: it is the outer garment (ridā'). The second: it is the palm, the ring and the face. The third: the kohl and the ring; both were narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The fourth: the two "qalbs," which are the two bracelets, the ring and the kohl; this was said by al-Miswar ibn Makhramah. The fifth: the kohl, the ring and the henna; this was said by Mujahid. The sixth: the ring and the bracelet; this was said by al-Hasan. The seventh: the face and the two palms; this was said by al-Dahhak. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: the first opinion is more fitting, and Ahmad explicitly stated it, saying: the apparent adornment is the clothing, and every part of her is 'awrah, even the fingernail. This implies the prohibition of looking at any part of a non-related woman without an excuse. If there is an excuse, such as wanting to marry her or to bear witness concerning her, then in both cases he may look at her face only. As for looking at her without an excuse, it is not permissible, neither for desire nor for other reasons; and in this the face, the palms and the rest of the body are equal.

If it is said: then why does the prayer not become invalid by uncovering her face?

The answer: covering it involves hardship, so it is excused.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and let them draw their head-coverings over their chests﴾. The word is the plural of khimar, which is what a woman covers her head with. The meaning: let them cast their veils (maqani') ﴿over their chests﴾, so that by that they cover their hair, their earrings and their necks. Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and al-A'mash read "ʿalā juyūbihinna" with a kasra on the jim (jīyūbihinna). ﴿And not to display their adornment﴾, meaning the hidden one, whose explanation has already passed. ﴿except to their husbands﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they should not remove the jilbab and the khimar except before their husbands.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or their women﴾, meaning the Muslim women. Ahmad said: it is not lawful for a Muslim woman to uncover her head in front of the women of the dhimmis, and the Jewish and Christian women do not accept (i.e., do not restrain) a Muslim woman.

(p-33) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾. Our companions said: what is meant by this is the female slaves (imā'), not the male slaves. The companions of al-Shafi'i said: it includes male slaves, so it is permissible for a woman, in their view, to show to her male slave what she shows to her mahrams, because the school of al-Shafi'i holds that he is a mahram for her, whereas in our view he is not a mahram, and it is not permissible for him to look at any part of her other than her face and palms. Ahmad explicitly stated that he may look at the hair of his mistress. Qadi Abu Ya'la said: the reason the female slaves are mentioned in the verse is that one might suppose it is not permissible for her to show her adornment to female slaves, since those previously mentioned are free; when He mentioned the female slaves, the difficulty was removed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or the male attendants who are followers﴾. These are those who follow the people and remain with them for their support, or because they were raised among them.

The exegetes have six opinions concerning this "follower."

One of them: he is the foolish man whom a woman does not desire and a man does not feel jealous over; this was said by Qatadah. Likewise Mujahid said: he is the simpleton who wants food and does not want women. The second: he is the impotent (ʿinnīn); this was said by ʿIkrimah. The third: the mukhannath, who used to follow a man, serving him with his food, and was unable to approach women nor desired them; this was said by al-Hasan. The fourth: the aged elder (p-34) who has passed his prime. The fifth: the servant; these two were said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The sixth: the one who has no concern for women, whether due to old age, decrepitude or youth; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Munadi from our companions. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿ghayr﴾ is a description of "the followers." In this there is evidence that His saying ﴿or those their right hands possess﴾ means ﴿other than men having no desire﴾. The third: the kohl and the ring; both were narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. The answer: covering it involves hardship, so it is excused.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or their women﴾, meaning the Muslim women. Ahmad said: it is not lawful for a Muslim woman to uncover her head in front of the women of the dhimmis, and the Jewish and Christian women do not accept (i.e., do not restrain) a Muslim woman.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: the reason the female slaves are mentioned in the verse is that one might suppose it is not permissible for her to show her adornment to female slaves, since those previously mentioned are free; when He mentioned the female slaves, the difficulty was removed.

[p-39] The second: the condition of desiring chastity was stipulated only because compulsion is conceivable only when chastity is desired; as for when the woman does not desire chastity, she is inclined to prostitution by nature.

The third: *in* (if) means *idh* (when), and similar to it is: ﴿And leave what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:278], and ﴿And you will be superior if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:139].

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad recited: "*min ba'di ikrahihinna lahunna ghafurun rahim*" (after their compulsion, for them, is Forgiving and Merciful).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Clear verses﴾. Ibn 'Amir and the people of Kufa, except Abu Bakr and Aban, recited: "*mubayyinat*" (with a kasra under the ya') in both places in this surah [al-Nur 24:34, 24:46], and in the last surah of al-Talaq (65:11).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And an example from those who passed away before you﴾, that is, a likeness of their state to your state, O deniers. This is a warning to them that what befell the deniers before them may befall them.

[p-40] The words of His Most High, ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, have two interpretations.

The first: He is the guide of the people of the heavens and the earth. This was related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, and Anas ibn Malik also said it. The explanation is that *nur* (light) in the language means *diya'* (radiance), which is that by which sight reaches what it sees. So *nur* is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, because He is the one who guides the believers and makes clear to them what they are guided by, and all creation is guided by His light.

The second: He is the manager (*mudabbir*) of the heavens and the earth. This was said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "Allah *nawwara*" with a fatha on the *nun* and the *waw*, with the letters doubled (*tashdid*), and with a fatha on the *ra'*; "al-samawat" in the genitive (*khafd*), and "wa al-ard" in the accusative (*nasb*).

The words of His Most High, ﴿the likeness of His light﴾: concerning the pronoun of *al-kinaya* (the returning pronoun, the "ha'" in *nurih*) there are four opinions.

The first: it refers back to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The likeness of His guidance in the heart of the believer."

The second: it refers back to the believer, so the meaning is: the likeness of the light of the believer. This was said by Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: "Mathal nur man amana bihi" (the likeness of the light of the one who believed in Him).

The third: it refers back to Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by Ka'b.

The fourth: it refers back to the Qur'an. This was said by Sufyan.

As for *al-mishkah* (the niche), there are three opinions.

The first: it is the place of the wick (*fatilah*) in the lamp (*qindil*), which is like a tube (*unbub*); and *al-misbah* (the lamp) is the light. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: *al-mishkah* is the lamp (*qindil*), and *al-misbah* is the wick. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is the recess (*kuwwa*) that has no opening through, and *al-misbah* is the lamp (*siraj*). This was said by Ka'b. Likewise al-Farra' said: *al-mishkah* is the recess that is not open through. Ibn Qutayba said: *al-mishkah* is the recess, in the language of Abyssinia (*al-Habasha*). Al-Zajjaj said: it is from the speech of the Arabs, and *al-misbah* is the lamp.

He mentioned *al-zujajah* (the glass) because light in glass is brighter than in anything else. Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi and Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "fi zujajatin al-zujajah" with a fatha on the *zay* in both places. Mu'adh al-Qari, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn Ya'mur read with a kasra on the *zay* in both places. Some of the scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: the meaning of the verse is "like a lamp in a niche," so it is an inversion (*maqlub*).

As for *al-durri*: Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Aban from 'Asim read *dirri'un* with a kasra on the *dal*, a lightened *ya'* (*takhfif*), and with a long vowel (*mamdud*) and a hamza (*mahmuz*). Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning according to this is that it is one of the shooting stars (*al-kawakib al-darari'*), which are those that *yadra'na 'alayk*, that is, they appear. Al-Zajjaj said: it is derived from *daraa yadra'u*, when it rushes off hurtling, so its light is multiplied. It is said: *tadara'a al-rajulan*, when the two men push against each other. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read *durriyyun* with a damma on the *dal*, a kasra on the *ra'*, and a doubled *ya'*, without a long vowel or a hamza. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read *dirri'un* with a fatha on the *dal*, a kasra on the *ra'*, with a long vowel and a hamza. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and Qatada read with a fatha on the *dal* and doubling on the *ra'* and the *ya'*, without a long vowel or a hamza. It is lit with olive wood, the Ibrisam (silk) is washed with its ash, its oil is extracted most easily, and its branch bears leaves from its beginning to its end. It was singled out for mention here rather than others because its oil is purer and brighter.

The second: it is in the open desert, which no mountain or cave shades, and nothing covers it, so its oil is better. 'Ikrima related it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise, as did al-Zajjaj.

The third: it is from the trees of Paradise, not from the trees of this world. This was said by al-Hasan.

[p-44] The first: to the light of the Qur'an. The second: to the light of faith (*iman*). The third: to the light of Muhammad (ﷺ). The fourth: to His religion, Islam.

**Fasl (section)**

As for the meaning of this parable, there are three opinions.

The first: it likened the light of Muhammad (ﷺ) to a shining lamp. So *al-mishkah* is the inside (*jawf*) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), *al-misbah* is the light that is in his heart, *al-zujajah* is his heart, and it is ﴿from a blessed tree﴾, which is Ibrahim (peace be upon him). He called it a blessed tree because most of the prophets came from his loins. ﴿Neither of the east nor of the west﴾: neither Jewish nor Christian. Muhammad (ﷺ) nearly makes clear to the people that he is a prophet even if he does not speak. Al-Qurazi said: *al-mishkah* is Ibrahim, *al-zujajah* is Isma'il, and *al-misbah* is Muhammad, may Allah bless him and them and grant them peace. Al-Dahhak said: He likened 'Abd al-Muttalib to the niche, 'Abd Allah to the glass, and Muhammad (ﷺ) to the lamp.

The second: it likened the light of faith in the heart of the believer to the lamp. So *al-mishkah* is his heart, and *al-misbah* is the light of faith in it. It was also said: *al-mishkah* is his chest, and *al-misbah* is the Qur'an and faith which are in his chest, and *al-zujajah* is his heart. So it is as if, by what is in it of Qur'an and faith, it is a shining star lit from a tree, which is sincerity (*ikhlas*). The likeness of sincerity with him is like a tree that the sun does not touch. Likewise this believer has guarded himself against being touched by trials. If he is given, he gives thanks; if he is tested, he is patient; if he speaks, he is truthful; if he judges, he is just. The heart of the believer acts by guidance before knowledge comes to him, and when knowledge comes to him his guidance increases, ﴿light upon light﴾, just as this oil nearly gives light before the fire touches it; when the fire touches it, its light is intensified. So the believer's speech is light, his deed is light, his entrance is light, his exit is light, and his destination is to light on the Day of Resurrection.

The third: it likened the Qur'an to a lamp by which one is illumined and which is not diminished. The glass is the heart of the believer, and the niche is his tongue and mouth. The blessed tree is the tree of revelation; the proofs of the Qur'an nearly become clear even if we do not recite it. It was also said: the proofs of Allah nearly give light to whoever reflects on them and contemplates them, even if the Qur'an had not been sent down. ﴿Light upon light﴾: that is, the Qur'an is a light from Allah for His creation, together with the evidences and signs that were established for them before the revelation of the Qur'an.

The words of His Most High, ﴿And Allah sets forth parables for the people﴾: that is, Allah makes clear the likenesses for the people, bringing them near to understanding and facilitating the paths of comprehension.

(p-46) The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿In houses﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "The word *fi* (in) belongs with His words ﴿like a niche﴾, so the meaning is: like a niche in houses. It is also possible that it connects with His words ﴿in which He is glorified﴾, so that *fiha* (in them) is a repetition for emphasis, and the meaning is: men glorify Allah in houses."

If it is asked: the niche is only in one house, so how does He say ﴿in houses﴾?

There are two answers to this. The first is that it is from the *khitab mutalawwin* (the shifting mode of address, a style that opens with the singular and closes with the plural), like His words: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq 65:1].

The second is that it refers to each of the houses, so the meaning is: in each house there is a niche. The commentators have three opinions on what is meant by "houses" here.

The first is that they are the mosques. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and by the majority of scholars. The second is that they are the houses of the wives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This was said by Mujahid. The third is that it is the House of the Holy Land (Bayt al-Maqdis). This was said by al-Hasan.

As for ﴿He has permitted﴾ (adhina), its meaning is "he has commanded." Regarding the meaning of ﴿that they be raised﴾, there are two opinions:

The first is that they be honored. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

The second is that they be built. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The first is His Oneness. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. The second is that His Book be recited in them. This was narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The first is the obligatory prayer. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ata. Salim narrated from Ibn Umar that he was in the market when the prayer was called, so they closed their shops and entered the mosque. Ibn Umar said: "It is concerning them that this was revealed: ﴿men whom neither trade nor sale distracts from the remembrance of Allah﴾."

The second is from standing in fulfillment of Allah's right. This was said by Qatadah.

The third is the remembrance of Allah by the tongue. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi mentioned this.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and the establishment of prayer﴾, i.e., performing it at its time and completing it.

If it is asked: if the intended meaning of the remembrance of Allah is the prayer, what is the purpose of repeating it?

The answer: He clarified that they establish it by performing it at its time.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿a Day when hearts and eyes will be turned about﴾. Regarding its meaning there are three opinions.

The first is that whoever's heart is a believer in the resurrection and the rising, his insight increases by seeing what he was promised; and whoever's heart is otherwise, sees what makes him certain of the matter of the Resurrection. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second is that hearts turn between hope of salvation and fear of destruction, and eyes turn, looking from where they will be given their records: from the right side or from the left? And from which direction they will be taken: from the right side or from the left? This was said by Ibn Jarir.

The third is that hearts turn until they reach the throats, and eyes turn to the blue-tinged glance after kohl, and blindness after sight.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿that He may reward them﴾. The meaning is: they glorify Allah so that He may reward them ﴿with the best of what they did﴾, i.e., He rewards them for their good deeds, and does not reward them for their misdeeds. ﴿And increase them from His bounty﴾ (p-49) what they did not deserve by their deeds. ﴿And Allah provides for whom He wills without account﴾. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 24, verses 39–40:

Then God struck a parable for the disbelievers, saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-sarab (mirage) is what you see of the sun, like water, at midday; al-aal (shimmering haze) is what you see at the beginning and end of the day, and it lifts up everything. Al-qay'ah and al-qa' are one and the same. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read: "bi-qay'at" (in plural). Al-Zajjaj said: al-qay'ah is the plural of qa', like jar and jiyrah (neighbours). Al-qay'ah and al-qa' are the flat land that is spread out and has no vegetation. The one who walks through it sees as if there were flowing water in it, and that is the mirage. Al-aal is like the mirage, except that it rises at the time of forenoon, like water, between the sky and the earth. The thirsty one, who is the one intensely parched with thirst, supposes it to be water; until, when he comes to the place of the mirage, he finds land with no water in it. So God informed that the disbeliever who thinks that his deed has benefited him with God is like the one who supposes the mirage to be water, and his deed has come to nothing.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿and he finds God with him﴾, meaning he arrives before God, ﴿and He pays him his account in full﴾, meaning He recompenses him for his deed. Outwardly this is a report about the thirsty one, but what is intended is a report about the disbeliever.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And God is swift at reckoning﴾ has been explained in (al-Baqarah: 202).

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Or like darkness﴾. Regarding this parable there are two opinions.

One: it is for the deeds of the disbeliever. This was said by the majority, and al-Zajjaj chose it.

The second: it is a parable for the heart of the disbeliever, in that it neither understands nor sees. This was said by al-Farra'. As for al-lujji, it is the one of great depth, the deep one. (Yaghshahu) meaning: that sea is covered over by ﴿a wave above it﴾, meaning above the first wave there is another wave, and the meaning is that wave follows wave until some of it is above other parts; ﴿above it﴾, meaning above that wave, ﴿is a cloud﴾.

Then he began, saying: ﴿darkness﴾, meaning the darkness of the sea, the darkness of the first wave, the darkness of the wave that is above the wave, and the darkness of the cloud. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read: "sahabu zulumatin" in the construct form. ﴿When he brings out his hand﴾, meaning: when someone brings it out, ﴿he almost cannot see it﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

One: he did not see it at all. This was said by al-Hasan and chosen by al-Zajjaj, who said: because in less than these darknesses the palm is not seen. Likewise Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is that he did not see it at all, because the evidence has been established by the description of the density of the darknesses that sight is absent. Thus it is made clear by this statement that "yakad" (almost) is here an emphatic extra particle, like what is in His words: ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 40].

The second: he did not see it except after great effort. This was said by al-Mubarrad. Al-Farra' said: this is like when you say: "I almost did not reach you," and you have arrived. Al-Farra' said: this is the grammatical sense of the Arabic.

One: religion and faith. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second: guidance. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 24, verse 41–42:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that to Allah prostrate [in worship] whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾. Its interpretation has already preceded [Al-Baqarah: 30].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the birds﴾, meaning: and the birds glorify Him, ﴿in ranks﴾, meaning: spreading their wings in the air. He specified the birds for mention because when they fly they are between the sky and the earth, so they are outside the whole of what is in the heavens and the earth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Each [of them] has known his prayer and his glorification﴾. Meaning: of the category he mentioned. The scholars of tafsir said: the prayer (salah) is for the children of Adam, and the glorification (tasbih) is for the other creatures.

Regarding the referent of His saying ﴿has known﴾ there are two views.

One of them: it is Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is: Allah has known the prayer and glorification of the one who prays and glorifies. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is the one who prays and glorifies. Then there are two views on this. One of them: the one who prays and glorifies has known his own prayer and glorification, that is, he has come to know what he was charged with of that. The second: the one who prays has known the prayer and glorification of Allah, that is, he knows that these belong to Allah alone, Exalted.

Qatadah, Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn Yamur read: "Each has been known" (kullun qad 'ulima), with the ʿayn raised and the lam kasra, "his prayer and his glorification" with the raf' (nominative) on both.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 24, verse 43–44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not seen that Allah drives the clouds﴾, meaning: drives them along (yasuquhu). ﴿Then brings them together﴾, meaning: joins some of them to others, so that the scattered pieces become one piece. The word "saḥāb" (cloud) has the form of a singular, but its meaning is plural; therefore He said: ﴿brings them together, then makes them into layers (rukām)﴾, meaning: He makes some of the clouds upon others. ﴿Then you see the rain (wadq)﴾, which is the rain. Al-Layth said: "al-Wadq" is rain, all of it, heavy and light.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿from within it (khilālihi)﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak recited: "min khalalihi". Al-Khilal is the plural of khalal, like jibal and jabal. ﴿And He sends down from the sky﴾: the object of "sending down" (al-inzal) is omitted; its implied meaning is: "and He sends down from the sky, from mountains in it of hail, hail", so He dispensed with mentioning the object because of the indication of it. The first "min" (from) denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah), because the beginning of the descent is from the sky; the second "min" denotes partiality (tab'idh), because what Allah sends down is a part of those mountains; and the third "min" denotes specification of the kind (tabyin al-jins), because the kind of those [mountains] (p-53) is the kind of hail. The exegetes said: they are mountains in the sky, created from hail. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the speech is: "and He sends down from the sky, from mountains of hail in it, just as you say: 'This is a ring on my hand of iron', meaning: this is an iron ring on my hand."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So He strikes with it﴾, meaning: with the hail, ﴿whom He wills﴾, so it harms his crops and fruits. Al-sana' is the light. ﴿Nearly takes away﴾. Mujahid and Abu Ja'far recited: "yudhhibu" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha'. ﴿Allah alternates the night and the day﴾, meaning: He brings this and takes away that. ﴿Indeed in that﴾ alternation ﴿is a lesson for those of vision﴾, meaning: a proof for people of insight and intellect of the oneness of Allah and His power.

The Qur'anic text in this passage is: ﴿And God created every creature﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: "And God is the Creator of every creature from water." There are two views about "water."

The first is that water is the origin of every creature. The second is that it refers to the nutfah (the sperm drop), and the intended meaning is all the animals observed in this world. He said ﴿among them﴾ by giving precedence to the rational beings (taghlib). He did not mention the one that walks on more than four because, to the eye, it is like the one that walks on four; it was also said that it relies on four in walking. He called the one that moves on its belly "walking" because every thing that moves along and continues is called "walking" (māshin), even if it is not an animal, to the extent that it is said: "This matter has walked (qad mashā hādhā al-amr)." This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Abu 'Ubayda said: this is only by way of comparison to the one who walks, because walking does not occur on the belly; it occurs only for one who has legs. When they mix what has legs with what has no legs, that is permitted, as they say: "I ate bread (khubzan) and milk (laban)," and one does not say "I ate milk" alone. (p-54)

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 24, verses 46–52:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they say, "We believe in Allah"﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir, the science of Qur'anic exegesis) said: It was revealed concerning a man from among the hypocrites called Bishr, who had a dispute with a Jew. The Jew invited the hypocrite to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to judge between them. The hypocrite said to the Jew, "Muhammad is unjust toward us!" But [he said], "Rather, [let us go to] Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf between you and me." Then this verse was revealed.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then a party of them turn away﴾, meaning the hypocrites, ﴿after that﴾, meaning after their saying "We believe." ﴿And those are not believers﴾, meaning those who turn away from the judgment of Allah and His Messenger. ﴿And when they are called to Allah﴾, meaning to His Book, ﴿and His Messenger, that he may judge between them,﴾ [the Messenger], ﴿behold, a party of them turn away.﴾ The meaning of the statement is that they used to turn away from the Messenger's judgment against them, because they knew that he judges by the truth. If the truth was in their favour against others, they hastened to his judgment, submitting, because they were confident that he would judge in their favour by the truth. Al-Zajjaj said: Idh'an (submission) in the language means hastening with obedience. You say, "He has submitted to me (adh'ana li)," meaning he has complied with me in what I was seeking from him.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is there in their hearts a disease﴾, meaning disbelief, ﴿or have they doubted﴾, meaning did they doubt the Qur'an? This is a question of blame and rebuke, and the meaning is that they are indeed like that. He expressed it in the form of a question so that it would be more emphatic in censuring them, as Jarir said in praise:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts,
And the most generous of the worlds in offering wine?"

meaning: You are indeed like that. As for al-hayf, it is inclination in judgment. It is said: "He deviated (hāfa) in his judgment," meaning he acted unjustly. ﴿Rather, they are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning Allah and His Messenger do not wrong anyone. Rather, they are wrongdoers against themselves through disbelief and turning away from the Messenger's judgment.

Then He described the believers, saying: ﴿The only saying of the believers﴾. Al-Farra' said: This is not a report of a past event; rather the meaning is: the saying of the believers should be, when they are called, that they say, "We hear and obey." Al-Hasan and Abu al-Jawza recited (qara'a, read) "innama kana qawlu al-mu'minin" with the lam in the nominative (damma). Abu Ja'far, Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn Abi [Layla] recited "liyuhkama baynahum" with a raised yā' and an open kāf (i.e., in the passive). The exegetes said: The meaning is: "We heard the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and obeyed his command," even if that was in what they disliked.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And fears Allah﴾, meaning regarding his past sins, ﴿and keeps his duty to Him﴾, meaning regarding what he may disobey Him in afterward. Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Warsh from Nafi' recited "wa-yattaqihi" (with a connected yā' ending, i.e., with the long vowel), (p-56) connected with a yā'. Qalun from Nafi' related "wa-yattaqhi fa-ulā'ika" with a kasra on the hā' without extending it to a yā'. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from Asim recited "wa-yattaqihi" with a jazm (sukun, the pausal vowelless ending).

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 24, verses 55–56**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised those among you who believe﴾. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Hakim narrated in his *Sahih*, from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions came to Madinah and the Ansar sheltered them, the Arabs threw them into a single bow (i.e., they united against them). They would not spend the night except with their weapons, and would not rise in the morning except in their armour. So they said: "Do you think we will live until we spend a night secure and at peace, fearing no one but Allah, Mighty and Majestic?" Then this verse was revealed.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, granted His Messenger victory over the Arabian Peninsula, they laid down their weapons and felt secure. Then Allah took His Prophet (ﷺ). They remained secure in this state during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, 'Umar and 'Uthman, until they fell into what they fell into and disbelieved in the blessing. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought fear upon them, and they changed, so Allah, Exalted is He, changed what was with them.

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this promise was made by Allah to the Ummah of Muhammad in the Torah and the Gospel.

Muqatil claimed that when the disbelievers of Makkah prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the Muslims from performing 'Umrah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, the Muslims said: "If only Allah, Exalted is He, would open Makkah to us." Then this verse was revealed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will surely make them successors﴾, meaning: He will surely make them succeed those who came before them. The meaning is: He will surely make them inherit the lands of the disbelievers, from among the Arabs and non-Arabs, and He will make them its rulers, governors and inhabitants. According to Muqatil's view, the "land" here refers to Makkah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited *kama istukhlifa* (as He was made successors), with a damma on the taa' and a kasra on the lam (i.e., the passive form). It refers to the Children of Israel. That is because, when the tyrants in Egypt were destroyed, Allah gave them their land, their homes and their wealth as an inheritance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion﴾, which is Islam. Its establishment (*tamkin*) is its manifestation over every other religion. ﴿And He will surely change [their state] for them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Aban and Ya'qub recited *wa-liyubdilanna* (with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal), meaning: ﴿from after their fear, security﴾, because they had been oppressed and subdued. ﴿They worship Me﴾: this is a new sentence in praise of them. ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that﴾, in these blessings, meaning: denies their rights. The exegetes said: The first to disbelieve in these blessings were the murderers of 'Uthman.

The meaning is: He will surely make them inherit the lands of the disbelievers, from among the Arabs and non-Arabs, and He will make them its rulers, governors and inhabitants. According to Muqatil's view, the "land" here refers to Makkah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿as He made successors of those before them﴾. Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited *kama istukhlifa* (as He was made successors), with a damma on the taa' and a kasra on the lam (i.e., the passive form). It refers to the Children of Israel. That is because, when the tyrants in Egypt were destroyed, Allah gave them their land, their homes and their wealth as an inheritance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He will surely establish for them their religion﴾, which is Islam. Its establishment (*tamkin*) is its manifestation over every other religion. ﴿And He will surely change [their state] for them﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, Aban and Ya'qub recited *wa-liyubdilanna* (with a sukun on the ba' and a light dal), meaning: ﴿from after their fear, security﴾, because they had been oppressed and subdued. ﴿They worship Me﴾: this is a new sentence in praise of them. ﴿And whoever disbelieves after that﴾, in these blessings, meaning: denies their rights. The exegetes said: The first to disbelieve in these blessings were the murderers of 'Uthman.

Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah, on the authority of 'Asim, read "لا يَحْسَبَنَّ" (lā yaḥsabanna) with a ya' (yā') and a fatḥah on the sin (sīn). The rest read it with a ta' (tā') and a kasrah on the sin (sīn), "لا تَحْسَبَنَّ" (lā taḥsabanna).

Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-A'mash read عَوَراتٍ (ʿawarātin) with a fatha on the waw.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 24, verse 61:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind man⦁﴾ There are five opinions concerning the occasion of its revelation.

The first: When His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood⦁﴾ [An-Nisa': 29] was revealed, the Muslims refrained from eating with the sick, the chronically ill, the blind and the lame. They said: food is the best of wealth, and Allah Exalted has forbidden consuming wealth in falsehood, while the blind man cannot see where good food is, and the sick man cannot eat his fill. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Some people, when they went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), would leave the keys of their houses with the blind man, the lame man, the sick man and their relatives, and would instruct them to eat from what was in their houses if they were in need. But they would avoid eating from them, saying: "We fear that their hearts will not be content with that." So this verse was revealed. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The third: The lame and the blind used to refrain from eating with the healthy, because people found them repulsive. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The fourth: A group of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they did not have anything to feed the sick or the disabled, would take him to the houses of their fathers, their mothers, and some of those whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, named in this verse. The disabled would feel uneasy about eating that food, because its giver was not its owner. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Mujahid.

The fifth: It was revealed concerning the exemption of the disabled mentioned in the verse from jihad. This was said by al-Hasan and Ibn Yazid.

According to the first opinion, the meaning of the verse is: there is no blame upon you regarding the blind man that you eat with him, nor regarding the lame man; and "ʿalā" (upon) carries the meaning of "fī" (in). This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. The meaning of the verse comes out in accordance with each opinion in a manner fitting to it. A group of the exegetes held that the statement ends at ﴿nor upon the sick man is there blame⦁﴾ and that what follows is a new statement with no connection to it. This strengthens the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you eat from your houses⦁﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: They are the houses of the children.

The second: The houses they live in while they are dependents of others. The address is then to a man's household, his son, his servant, and whoever his dwelling includes, and it is attributed to them because they are its inhabitants.

The third: They are their own houses, and what is meant is their eating from the property of their dependants and wives, because a woman's house is like a man's house.

He permitted eating from the houses of the relatives mentioned only because it is customary for them to offer their food to them. If the food is behind a protected storage (hirz), it is not permissible to break the protection.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or what you possess the keys of⦁﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: It refers to the agent (wakil); there is no harm in his eating a small amount. This is the meaning of the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu al-'Aliyah recited it as "mulliktum" with a damma on the mim and a shadda on the lam, with a kasra, in the passive form. Sa'id explained it, saying: it means the steward (qahramān) who holds the keys in his hand.

Anas ibn Malik, Qatadah and Ibn Ya'mur recited "miftahahu" with a kasra on the mim, in the singular.

The second: The house of the person, which he owns. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

The third: The houses of the slaves. This was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or your friend⦁﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: This was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn 'Amr, who went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to fight, and left Malik ibn Zayd in charge of his family. When he returned, he found him exhausted, and said: "I felt uneasy about eating from your food without your permission." So this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan and Qatadah held that eating from a friend's food without asking permission is permissible.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together or separately⦁﴾ Concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse there are three opinions.

The first: A tribe from Banu Kinanah called Banu Layth used to be scrupulous about a man eating food alone; a man might sit with food before him from morning until evening. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The second: A group of the Ansar would not eat when a guest came to them except together with their guest. So this verse was revealed, and they were given permission to eat together or in separate groups. This was said by 'Ikrimah.

The third: The Muslims used to be scrupulous about eating with the people of hardship, fearing that they would take more for themselves over them, and about gathering around food because people differ in what they eat and in how much some have over others. So this was made easy for them. It was said: ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together⦁﴾ meaning gathered, ﴿or separately⦁﴾ meaning dispersed. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you enter houses⦁﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: They are your own houses; so greet your families and dependants. This was said by Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Tawus and Qatadah.

The second: They are mosques; so greet those within them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: Houses of others; the meaning is: when you enter the houses of others, greet them. This was said by al-Hasan.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a greeting⦁﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), because His saying ﴿so greet⦁﴾ carries the sense of: "so greet, and let one of you greet another with a greeting." ﴿from Allah⦁﴾ Muqatil said: blessed with reward. ﴿good⦁﴾ meaning: fine.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they are with him﴾, meaning: with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿upon a matter of gathering﴾, i.e., upon a matter of obedience that they gather for, such as jihad, the Friday prayer (jumu'ah), the festival (eid), and the like. ﴿They do not go away until they have asked his permission.﴾ The exegetes said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ascended the pulpit (minbar) on the day of Friday (p-68), and a man wished to leave the mosque for a need or an excuse, he would not leave until he stood opposite the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) where he could see him, and he (the Prophet) would know that he had only stood up to seek permission, so he would grant permission to whomever he wished among them. The matter in that is up to him." Mujahid said: The permission of the imam on the day of Friday is that he gestures with his hand.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And ask forgiveness for them from Allah﴾, i.e., for their leaving the congregation, if you see that they have an excuse.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 24, verse 63–64:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among yourselves like the call of some of you to others﴾. Concerning this there are three views.

The first: it is a prohibition against provoking the anger of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), for when he calls down (a curse) upon a person, his supplication is binding. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they were commanded to say, "O Messenger of Allah," and forbidden to say, "O Muhammad." This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAlqamah, al-Aswad, ʿIkrimah, and Mujahid.

The third: it is a prohibition for them against delaying when he commands them and against lagging behind when he calls them. This is related by al-Mawardi.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Muʿadh al-Qari recited: "duʿaa'a al-rasūli nabiyyikum," with a shadda on the yāʾ and a nūn before the bāʾ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away﴾. Tasallul (تَسَلُّل) means leaving in secrecy.

(p-69) And liwādh (لِواذ) means concealing oneself behind something for fear of being seen by someone. The meaning of His saying ﴿Allah already knows﴾ is a warning of requital. Al-Farra' said: "The hypocrites used to attend the Friday prayer, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would mention them and reproach them with the verses that were revealed about them. If one of them could slip away unnoticed, he would stand up and leave. This is His saying: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away, hiding behind one another (liwādh)﴾," meaning one of them takes cover behind another, i.e., one conceals himself with another.

Likewise Tha'lab said: the form was built upon lāwadha, mulāwadhah; had it been built upon lādha yalūdhu, it would have been said liyādhan. It was also said: this occurred during the digging of the trench, when the hypocrites would depart without the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), hiding themselves.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾. Concerning the pronoun of reference (hāʾ al-kināyah) there are two views.

The first: it refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah.

Concerning ʿan (عَنْ) there are two views.

The first: it is extra (zāʾidah). This is the view of al-Akhfash. The second: the meaning of ﴿yukhalifūna﴾ is "they turn away from his command."

Concerning fitnah here there are three views.

The first: misguidance; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: a trial in this world; this is the view of Mujahid. The third: disbelief; this is the view of al-Suddi and Muqatil.

The first: killing in this world. The second: the punishment of Hell in the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what you are upon﴾, i.e., what is in your souls and what your hearts conceal of faith and hypocrisy. This is an admonition regarding the requital for that.
